This is not a defeater, because the separation face IS the root residue (its other pole), and these uses never denote anything but the demarcating interval — they never drift to an unrelated sense. A second potential resister, tabayyana meaning "verify/ascertain" (49:6, 4:94), is reconciled: to ascertain is to seek the distinction of true from false — the make-distinct residue in an epistemic-imperative construction, confirmed by 2:256/2:187 where tabayyana + min is literally "become distinct from."

Alh.candidate_root_contribution: Deity-hood: the status/category of being a god — an entity set up or invoked as an object of worship. The root names the DEITY-slot itself (the thing that is a god), independent of whether the claim to divinity is affirmed (Allah) or denied (the idols). It is entity-categorial, not the relational lordship of r-b-b nor the worship-act of ʕ-b-d.
Alh.plain_explanation: Every one of the 2851 occurrences is either the common noun ilah / plural aliha ("a deity / deities," 147 = form N) or the proper name Allah / vocative Allahumma ("God," 2704 = form PN). Both surface families denote the same thing at bottom: a being named as a god. Allah is the one true deity (the sole legitimate ilah); the plural aliha are the false gods the idolaters name and worship; the negated singular in "la ilaha illa..." asserts there is no deity but the one; the interrogative "a-ilahun maʕa llah" ("is there a deity alongside Allah?") challenges rival deity-claims. In each, once you subtract case/number, proclitics (wa-, bi-, li-, ta-, fa-), interrogative hamza, and construction, what remains is the same residue: "that which is (taken as) a god."
Alh.strongest_counterexample: The proper name Allah itself (2704 occurrences, ~95% of the data). One can argue a rigid-designator proper name has subtracted its descriptive residue entirely, leaving pure reference — the way "God" as a personal name need not actively predicate "is a deity." If that view is taken, the deity residue is not DEMONSTRABLY present in the bulk of occurrences but only etymologically assumed, and universal presence would rest on an unverifiable claim about a frozen name. This does not surface as an incoherent occurrence (no verse uses Allah to mean anything non-divine), but it is the point where the residue is weakest / least independently observable.

xyr.candidate_root_contribution: The status of being the preferred/superior good: that which is (or would be) singled out over alternatives as the more choiceworthy/beneficial option; and, in the verbal derivations, the act of singling that preferred thing out (to choose/select). Residue = PREFERENCE-OF-THE-GOOD (choiceworthiness).
xyr.plain_explanation: Every kh-y-r word in the set turns on one axis: that which is preferred because it is good (the better, the best, the choiceworthy), and in the verbs the act of singling that out. The comparative khayrun-min ("better than": 38:76 Iblis "I am better than him", 97:3 "better than a thousand months", 2:221, 27:36) names X as the preferred term of a comparison. The construct khayru + genitive-plural ("best of judges/providers/creation": 10:109, 22:58, 98:7; 3:110 khayra ummatin "best community") names the topmost of a class. Bare khayr ("good/benefit/wealth": 100:8 love of khayr, 2:180 "if he leaves khayr", 2:215, 22:36 "in them is khayr for you", 70:21 "khayr touches him") names the desirable-good one loves, spends, is touched by. Khayrat ("good things/deeds": 2:148 and 5:48 "race to the khayrat", 21:90, 23:61, 9:88) names the choiceworthy things one competes for. The verbs (Form VIII ikhtara/ikhtartuka: 20:13, 44:32 "over the worlds", 7:155 "singled out as preferred"; Form V yatakhayyarun/takhayyarun: 56:20, 68:38 "pick what they prefer"; and al-khiyarah: 28:68, 33:36 "the prerogative of choice") enact that same preference as an act of selection. Across all 196 the root supplies the preferred-good; form, construction and context supply the comparison, superlative frame, referent or agency.
xyr.strongest_counterexample: khayru al-makirin "best of schemers" (3:54, 8:30) and Iblis's ana khayrun minhu "I am better than him" (7:12, 38:76). In the first, the class (makr) is not itself morally good, yet the root still contributes "the pre-eminent/most-effective of the class" (superiority/preference), with the valence supplied by context, not the root. In the second, the claim is false, yet the root still contributes an asserted superiority/preferability; the falsehood is contextual, not a different root sense. Neither breaks universal presence: preference-of-the-superior remains the residue.

Hsn.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes a single positive evaluative quality: the state of being — or the act of rendering — GOOD / FINE / FAIR / COMELY / EXCELLENT. It marks the "good/fine" pole of an evaluative axis whose opposite pole the Quran names with سوء / سيّئة (and, aesthetically, قبح). This one quality surfaces both aesthetically (beauty, comeliness, fairness) and morally/qualitatively (goodness, excellence, best-ness); the two are not separate meanings but the same evaluative fineness applied to appearance versus conduct/outcome.
Hsn.plain_explanation: Every ح-س-ن word in the packet says that something is good/fine, is made good/fine, or is the best/finest. The forms distribute the same core quality across grammatical slots. ADJ حَسَن/حِسَان predicates the quality of a noun: رزقًا حسنًا "goodly provision" (11:88, 16:67, 22:58), خيراتٌ حِسانٌ "fair maidens" (55:70), عبقريٍّ حِسانٍ "fine carpets" (55:76), الأسماء الحُسنى "the finest names" (7:180, 17:110, 20:8, 59:24), أسوةٌ حسنةٌ "a good example" (33:21, 60:4, 60:6), قرضًا حسنًا "a goodly loan" (2:245, 57:11, 64:17, 73:20). N حَسَنة nominalizes it as "a good thing/deed," repeatedly and explicitly opposed to سيّئة (13:22, 41:34, 4:78-79, 27:46, 28:54, 7:168 بالحسنات والسيّئات). The elative أَحْسَن = "better/finest/best" (أحسن القصص 12:3, أحسن الحديث 39:23, أحسن تقويم 95:4, بالتي هي أحسن 6:152/17:34/29:46). The superlative feminine الحُسْنَى = "the best (reward/outcome)" (10:26, 53:31, 92:6/92:9, 4:95, 57:10). حُسْن = "goodness/fineness" (حسنُ مآب 13:29, حُسنُهنّ "their beauty" 33:52). The Form-IV verb أَحْسَن and its verbal noun إِحْسَان = "to make good / to do good / excellence" (أحسن كل شيء خلقه 32:7, فأحسن صوركم 40:64/64:3, أحسن مثواي 12:23, بالوالدين إحسانًا, هل جزاء الإحسان إلا الإحسان 55:60), and the participle مُحْسِن/المُحْسِنِين = "doer(s) of good." The stative Form-I حَسُنَ = "is/became good/excellent" (حَسُنَت مرتفقًا 18:31, حَسُنَت مستقرًّا 25:76, حَسُنَ أولئك رفيقًا 4:69). Subtract the form and the constant is always the good/fine/excellent quality.
Hsn.strongest_counterexample: 18:104 (وهم يحسبون أنهم يُحسنون صُنعًا, "they reckon they are doing good in work") and 35:8 (فرآه حسنًا, an evil deed that its doer "sees as good/fine"). Here the good-quality is FALSELY attributed to something actually bad. This does not break presence: the root still denotes exactly the "good/fine" quality — it is merely predicated wrongly (subjectively claimed/perceived). The word means "good"; the falsehood lies in the predication, not in a shift of the root's contribution. A second, distinctness-testing case is the recurring pairing خيرٌ وأحسن (17:35, 4:59) and أحسن مقيلًا / خير مستقرًّا (25:24), where أحسن can look synonymous with خير — but the very co-occurrence shows the Quran treats them as distinct facets (benefit/welfare = خير, fineness/excellence = أحسن), which supports rather than dissolves the residue.

Tyb.candidate_root_contribution: Root ط ي ب contributes an intrinsic POSITIVE QUALITY of a referent: being wholesome / agreeable / pure / good — pleasing to sense, sound moral judgment, or appetite, and free of contamination or foulness. Its defining anchor is the repeated explicit contrast with خبيث (khabith = foul/corrupt/impure). The residue is NOT "lawful," "beautiful in form," or "sound/fit-for-purpose," but the wholesome-agreeable-pure goodness intrinsic to the thing itself.
Tyb.plain_explanation: Across all 50 occurrences the word tags something as "good" in the sense of clean, wholesome, agreeable and unspoiled. Food/provision is "the good things" (الطيبات) that are wholesome to eat; speech can be "good/pure" (كلمة طيبة, الكلم الطيب, الطيب من القول); a wind is "favorable/pleasant" (ريح طيبة); earth for dry ablution is "clean/pure" (صعيدا طيبا); offspring, a life, dwellings, a land and a greeting are "good/wholesome"; the dying believers are received "in a good/pure state" (طيبين); and the verb طاب means "to be/become good, pleasing, or willingly content." Everywhere the root marks agreeable wholesome purity — the opposite of the foul (خبيث), which stands as its named antonym in six verses.
Tyb.strongest_counterexample: 4:4 فإن طِبْنَ لكم عن شيء منه نفسًا ("if they, of their own good pleasure, remit to you part of it"). Here the root shifts from an intrinsic quality of a thing to the volitional pleasedness/contentment of a self. It is still reconcilable: the residue is the "good/agreeable" state — the self being genuinely well-pleased and willing — the psychological instance of tayyib (cf. نفسًا "as to self"). A related edge case is صعيدا طيبا (4:43, 5:6) where the sense narrows to "ritually clean/pure earth," but purity is a core face of the same residue and is confirmed by the tayyib/khabith purity axis elsewhere. Neither breaks universal presence; both instantiate wholesome-agreeable-pure goodness rather than contradict it.

fsd.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the undoing or absence of sound, functioning integrity: the passage of some ordered/wholesome state into ruin, spoilage, breakdown, disorder. It is the counter-state to ص ل ح (soundness/being-set-right). Intransitively it is "to fall into ruin/disorder" (a system losing its working coherence); causatively/agentively it is "to bring to ruin, to spoil, to work corruption." The invariant is not an act of destruction per se but the resulting loss of a sound, integral order.
fsd.plain_explanation: Every one of the 50 occurrences turns on one idea: a sound, working order being spoiled or falling apart — the opposite of things being set right (صلاح). Three verb-forms describe the cosmos itself "going to ruin" if it had multiple gods (21:22, 23:71, 2:251) — pure, agent-free breakdown of ordered functioning. The Form IV verbs and the participle مفسدون/مفسدين describe people who "bring ruin" in the land (spreading disorder, bloodshed, cutting ties, mismanaging orphans' estates). The noun فساد names the ruined state itself ("corruption appeared on land and sea," 30:41). Whether spontaneous (heavens/earth) or caused (people in the earth), the shared residue is: the loss/undoing of a sound, integral order.
fsd.strongest_counterexample: 2:220 (ٱلْمُفْسِدَ مِنَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِ) is the mildest, non-violent case — merely mismanaging/spoiling an orphan's estate, with no "corruption in the land" crime-scene. It could tempt a narrower "large-scale social evil" gloss, but it in fact confirms the residue: the mufsid is precisely the one who spoils/ruins the affair as against the one who sets it right, matching the antonymy exactly. The disciplining case in the other direction is 21:22 لَفَسَدَتَا (heavens and earth "would go to ruin"): it has no moral agent, so it forbids reading the root as "evildoing" and forces the neutral "breakdown of sound order."

nfE.candidate_root_contribution: The bringing-about of benefit/advantage that accrues to a recipient — the positive functional-good pole (usefulness, profit, gain that reaches a beneficiary), standing as the antonymic counterpart of ضرّ (harm).
nfE.plain_explanation: Across all 50 occurrences the root نفع denotes conferring benefit/advantage on someone — something proving useful or profitable to a recipient. This shows up as a verb (يَنْفَع "benefits X"), as an abstract noun (نَفْع "benefit"), and as a concrete plural (مَنَافِع "uses/benefits" — of cattle, iron, wine, the pilgrimage). Whether the statement is positive (faith benefited the town 10:98; the reminder benefits believers 51:55; water/ships that benefit people 13:17, 2:164) or negative (idols that can neither benefit nor harm; intercession/faith/excuse/wealth that will not benefit on the Day), the same nucleus is present: advantage accruing to a beneficiary. Negated cases still fully presuppose the concept — they deny that benefit will materialize, which requires the concept of benefit.
nfE.strongest_counterexample: 57:25 مَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ ("and [in iron] benefits for people"), juxtaposed with بَأْسٌ شَدِيدٌ ("great might"). Here نفع is a concrete plural noun rather than a benefit/harm event, so one might ask whether it has drifted to mere "material commodity." But it holds: مَنَافِع are precisely the useful advantages iron confers on people (لِلنَّاسِ marks the beneficiary), i.e. the reified plural of the same residue. The eschatological negations (e.g. 74:48 شَفَاعَةُ الشَّافِعِينَ that does not benefit) are also non-resistant: they deny the accrual of benefit, which entails the concept.

Eql.candidate_root_contribution: The active mental operation of grasping and connecting input — signs, speech, or consequences — into an intelligible conclusion that ought to govern belief and conduct. Across all 49 occurrences the verb never denotes stored knowledge or a possessed fact; it denotes a *process* that is demanded of, exercised by, or absent in the subject: turning heard/seen/read evidence into a binding comprehension. This is why it recurs in the imperative-rebuke ("do you not then reason?"), the qualifier ("signs for a people who reason"), the purpose clause ("that you may reason"), and the accusation ("they do not reason"). Distinctively, when transitive its object is precisely something to be construed — the word of God (2:75 "after they had comprehended it"), the parables (29:43 "none comprehends them but the learned") — and its located organ is the heart (22:46 "hearts by which they reason"), while it is repeatedly set beside/above mere hearing (10:42, 25:44, 67:10, 2:75). The residue is therefore the connective-comprehending act, not the perception that feeds it nor the knowledge that might result.
Eql.plain_explanation: This root is one word used one way in all 49 places: a verb meaning "to use one's reason / to comprehend." God repeatedly points to natural signs (day and night, rain reviving the earth, sun and moon), to scripture, and to moral facts (the hereafter is better than this life), and then asks whether people "reason" — i.e. whether they actually connect the evidence in front of them to the obvious conclusion. People who fail to do this are compared to cattle (25:44), to the deaf-dumb-blind (2:171, 8:22), and to the worst of beasts (8:22). The word is never about having information; it is about the live act of grasping and joining the dots. That single sense fits every occurrence with no exceptions.
Eql.strongest_counterexample: 29:43 "وَمَا يَعْقِلُهَآ إِلَّا ٱلْعَٰلِمُونَ" — "none reason/comprehend them [the parables] except those who know." This is the strongest tension because it pairs the verb with ٱلْعَٰلِمُونَ (the knowers), risking collapse into "knowledge" (علم). But it in fact confirms the residue: the parables (هَا) are the object to be *construed*, and the verse distinguishes the act of construing them from the class of people (the learned) capable of it — reasoning is the operation, knowledge is the precondition, not the same thing. The other candidate, 22:46 "قُلُوبٌ يَعْقِلُونَ بِهَا" (hearts by which they reason), also holds: it names the organ/instrument of the act without altering the act itself.

$kk.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes a state of unsettled uncertainty: the mind held in suspension between alternatives, not firmly decided/convinced about the truth of some object-claim. In every occurrence it names a subject's non-settledness regarding a specific matter (a revelation, a religion, the Hereafter, a messenger's call, or God). After subtracting the noun form and its construction, the residue is "wavering / lack of firm conviction about X" — neither knowledge (علم/يقين) nor mere leaning (ظنّ), but an interior non-resolution.
$kk.plain_explanation: Every one of the 15 confirmed occurrences is the noun شَكّ ("doubt"). Fourteen appear in the locative construction (لـ)فِى شَكٍّ — "(they/you are) IN doubt" — treating doubt as a state one is inside of. The remaining one (14:10) is the nominative in a rhetorical question, أَفِى ٱللَّهِ شَكٌّ ("Is there any doubt about God?"), which presupposes there should be none — still the same noun with the same meaning. In each case the object of doubt is introduced by مِن / مِمَّا / مِنْه / مِنْها (about my religion 10:104, about what We sent down 10:94, about it 11:110, about what you call us to 11:62/14:9, about the Hereafter 27:66/34:21, about My reminder 38:8, about what came to you 40:34, about it 41:45/42:14/4:157). Two (34:54, 44:9) leave the object implicit but the context (revelation/the reckoning) is identical. The contribution — being unsettled/uncertain about a truth-claim — is demonstrably present in all 15.
$kk.strongest_counterexample: 14:10 — أَفِى ٱللَّهِ شَكٌّ ("Is there any doubt concerning God?"). This is the only non-فِى-شَكّ-state token: شَكّ is nominative subject of a rhetorical existential question, and its object is God's very reality rather than a revelation/message. It is also the only case where the verse's rhetorical thrust asserts doubt should NOT exist. Yet the lexical contribution is unchanged — the word still denotes uncertainty about a truth, and the rhetorical question only works because شَكّ means exactly "unsettled uncertainty." It does not resist the proposed residue; it confirms it by negation.

Hrj.candidate_root_contribution: An impassable tightness / constriction — a straitening that closes off room to move, breathe, or act. In its most literal packet witness (6:125, صدره ضيقا حرجا) it names an extreme narrowing of the chest; generalized, it is the binding, hemming-in that leaves no give.
Hrj.plain_explanation: The root ح ر ج carries the sense of being hemmed in with no room — a constricting tightness. You see it plainly where the Quran describes a chest made "narrow and حرجا" (6:125) or a constriction "in your chest" (7:2), and an inner tightness/resistance one might "find in oneself" about a judgment (4:65). The large family of legal verses all use the fixed formula "there is no حرج upon so-and-so" — over the blind, lame, sick, the weak, the Prophet, the believers (24:61, 48:17, 9:91, 33:37-50, 22:78, 5:6). There the same core sense operates: no constricting restriction/burden is laid upon them. The formula's "no ... upon" contributes the removal/exemption; the domain (religion, ablution, adoption law) is context; what is left in every case is the notion of a straitening tightness. Even the abstract legal uses read cleanly as "no binding constraint is placed on you," not as a separate meaning.
Hrj.strongest_counterexample: The purely legal-permission verses 33:37, 33:38, 33:50 are the hardest: there "no حرج upon the Prophet/the believers" concerning marrying adopted sons' ex-wives reads most naturally in English as "no blame/sin," which could suggest the root means culpability rather than constriction. However, the constriction reading still fits — the removal of a binding legal restriction that would otherwise hem the person in — and, decisively, 24:61 places حرج and جناح side by side in one verse, showing the Quran does not treat حرج as the blame-word (that is جناح); حرج is the straitening these persons are freed from.

Hrr.candidate_root_contribution: The strongest single candidate contribution is "being unbound / released from bondage or constraint — free." It is demonstrably present in two clusters on internal evidence: (a) al-Hurr / al-Hurr in 2:178, where the free person is explicitly set against al-'abd (the slave), and (b) the Form II tahriru raqabah cluster (4:92 x3, 58:3, 5:89) plus muharraran (3:35), where the act is making a slave-neck free / dedicating-releasing a child to God. Across these 8 occurrences the residue "release from bondage" survives after subtracting form and participants. However, this candidate is NOT present in the remaining 7 occurrences (heat: 16:81, 35:21, 9:81 x2; silk: 22:23, 35:33, 76:12), so it is not a universal contribution.
Hrr.plain_explanation: The root ح ر ر in the Quran breaks into three semantic islands that share only the three consonants, not a single demonstrable meaning: HEAT (al-harr, al-harur, harr — garments that protect from heat, scorching heat, Hellfire's intensity), SILK (harir — the fabric of Paradise), and FREEDOM (al-hurr = a free man vs. a slave; tahriru raqabah = freeing a slave; muharraran = a dedicated/released child). The freedom sense (8 of 15 occurrences) is internally coherent and even self-defines via its antonym 'slave.' But the heat sense (4) and silk sense (3) cannot be reduced to that freedom residue using only the verse evidence — nothing in "garments that guard you from the heat" or "their garment is silk" internally evokes release from bondage. Bridging heat, silk, and freedom would require outside etymology, which the rules forbid as evidence. Because whole clusters resist, universal presence fails.
Hrr.strongest_counterexample: 22:23 / 35:33 / 76:12 — harir (silk), a paradisal luxury fabric. It resists BOTH rival unifying hypotheses simultaneously: it carries no internal sense of "freedom/release" and no internal sense of "heat." A garment described only as fine cloth worn by the blessed offers nothing, on verse-internal grounds, that can be equated with either the free-vs-slave residue or the thermal residue. Silk therefore stands as an irreducible third island and single-handedly blocks universal presence.

Smm.candidate_root_contribution: Closure/imperviousness of the aural channel — the ear sealed shut so that sound, and specifically the call (al-du'a'), does not penetrate or register. The residue is not "not-hearing" as a bare negation but a stopped-up, blocked receptive channel: the sealed state that makes aural reception impossible.
Smm.plain_explanation: Every one of the 15 occurrences means "deaf / made deaf / became deaf." The shared root contribution across all of them is a BLOCKED HEARING CHANNEL — an ear stopped up so sound cannot get in. In 12 places it is the attribute/noun "the deaf" (as-summ, al-asamm, summan). Twice (5:71) it is the verb "they became deaf" (they closed their own ears). Once (47:23) it is causative "He made them deaf." The residue is stable and literal at the sensory level even when the reference is spiritual: disbelievers are likened to people whose ears are sealed to the call. Three times the object is explicitly al-du'a' (the call) — "the deaf do not hear the call" (21:45, 27:80, 30:52), which pins the residue to aural non-reception, not a general dullness.
Smm.strongest_counterexample: 25:73 — "lam yakhirru 'alayha summan wa 'umyanan" ("they do not fall upon them [the ayat] deaf and blind") — here summ describes the manner in which believers do NOT receive revelation. The reference is inverted (a negated/desired non-state) and abstract, so one might argue the sensory core is bleached. But even here the residue holds: the contrast is precisely between an ear sealed to the ayat versus one open to them; "deaf" still contributes blocked aural reception. Likewise 5:71 sammu is fully metaphorical, yet the pattern still denotes entering the sealed-hearing state. Neither dissolves the residue.

$Am.candidate_root_contribution: The root marks the LEFT side construed as the inauspicious / ill-omened / ill-fated direction — "left-handedness" carrying the coloring of doom and misfortune (as opposed to the blessed right). In all occurrences it names the damned cohort via the noun al-mash'amah, literally "the left(-hand side)."
$Am.plain_explanation: Every one of the 3 confirmed occurrences is the exact same word — الْمَشْـَٔمَة (al-mash'amah, maf'alah pattern) — in the exact same genitive phrase أَصْحَٰبُ الْمَشْـَٔمَةِ "the companions of the left/ill-omen." In 56:9 it appears twice (the emphatic doubling أصحاب المشأمة ما أصحاب المشأمة), and in 90:19 it labels those who disbelieved in God's signs. Across all three the word designates the doomed group placed on the ill-fated left side at the reckoning, in explicit or implicit contrast with أصحاب الميمنة ("the companions of the right", from the antonym root ي م ن). The root's contribution — the left as the ominous, damnation-marked direction — is present in every occurrence. However, because the evidence is a single word-type in a single construction repeated three times, the contribution cannot be tested across formal or contextual variation.
$Am.strongest_counterexample: There is no dissenting occurrence — but the strongest challenge is structural rather than a counterexample: all 3 tokens are one and the same lexeme (المشأمة) in one and the same construction (أصحاب المشأمة). Universal presence is therefore satisfied trivially, because there is only one word-type to satisfy it. No occurrence exercises a different form, a different collocation, or a non-eschatological sense, so the residue is never stress-tested. The nearest thing to a tension is 90:19, where the ill-omen coloring is discharged entirely by the surrounding كَفَرُوا clause, leaving open whether المشأمة itself contributes "ill-omen" or merely "left/the-left-group" with omen supplied contextually.

$Hn.candidate_root_contribution: Loading up / freighting to capacity — the act or resultant state of a vessel being packed with its cargo and passengers. The root residue is "being laden/freighted": filled by having a load put into it, not merely spatially full.
$Hn.plain_explanation: The root ش ح ن occurs in the Quran only three times, and in every case it is the same word: مَشْحُون, the passive participle describing الفلك (the ship) — "the laden ship." In 26:119 it is Noah's ark that saves him and those with him; in 36:41 it is the loaded ship carrying people's offspring as a sign; in 37:140 it is the ship Jonah flees to. Across all three the ship is characterized as loaded/freighted — packed with its load of people (and by narrative implication provisions/animals). The root's contribution across the full set is the notion of being loaded up to full capacity.
$Hn.strongest_counterexample: There is no resistant occurrence — all three tokens are the literally identical word مَشْحُون. The real weakness is not a counterexample but the total absence of variation: the root never appears outside الفلك المشحون, so nothing tests whether the residue is "loading with freight" specifically versus a more generic "filled/full." A hostile reading could claim the three tokens are one frozen lexical fossil, not evidence of a productive root contribution.

$TT.candidate_root_contribution: A departure that overshoots remotely far beyond the correct/proper limit — the spatial "far edge" sense (cf. shaṭṭ, the far riverbank) generalized to a bound of truth, justice, or measure. The residue is: going too far past the right mark.
$TT.plain_explanation: Across all 3 occurrences the root marks something that has gone far beyond the proper bound. In 18:14 and 72:4 it is a statement (object of a speech verb) that overshoots the truth about God — an extreme, far-fetched falsehood. In 38:22 it is a verb (Form IV) asking a judge not to overshoot the standard of just judgment ("judge with truth and do not shaṭaṭ"). Speech-excess vs. judicial-excess are different domains, but the same core "far past the correct limit" is present in each.
$TT.strongest_counterexample: 38:22 (تُشْطِط) is the hardest: read loosely it could mean simply "be unjust," collapsing the root into ظلم/جور and losing distinctiveness. But its pairing with "احكم بالحق" (judge with the truth) frames it as overshooting/deviating far from the truth-standard, preserving the "far beyond the mark" residue rather than a generic "do wrong." It reconciles.

$kw.candidate_root_contribution: The act of laying open / pouring out an inner distress or grievance and directing it outward toward a recipient for relief. Derived from the two verbal occurrences: 12:86 أَشْكُوا۟ (Form I) explicitly pairs the act with its inner object بَثِّى وَحُزْنِى ("my anguish and grief") and the recipient إِلَى ٱللَّهِ; 58:1 تَشْتَكِى (Form VIII) shows the same directional structure إِلَى ٱللَّهِ over a marital grievance. The residue after subtracting form and the إلى-recipient construction is: exposing-what-is-held-within-as-a-grievance to another.
$kw.plain_explanation: This root's clear meaning is "to complain / voice a grievance" — to take an inner pain or wrong and lay it open before someone who can address it. Both verb occurrences do exactly this, and both direct the complaint "to Allah" (إلى الله): Jacob pouring out his grief (12:86), and the woman appealing over her husband (58:1). The problem is the third occurrence, 24:35, which is not a verb of complaining at all but the noun مِشكاة — a "niche" or recess in a wall that holds a lamp. A niche has no grievance, no one complaining, and no recipient. To make the niche "fit" the complaint sense you have to reach outside the packet (to classical lexica about شكوة as a receptacle/waterskin, or to the loanword hypothesis for mishkāt), which the rules forbid as evidence. So the crisp contribution proven in two of three occurrences is genuinely absent from the third, and I cannot honestly claim universal presence.
$kw.strongest_counterexample: 24:35 كَمِشْكَوٰةٍ فِيهَا مِصْبَاحٌ — the noun مِشكاة is a lamp-niche/recess. Under the candidate contribution ("lay open an inner grievance to a recipient") there is nothing to reconcile: no complainant, no grievance, no directed appeal, and no addressee who grants relief. The only way to bridge it to the complaint sense is to substitute a far more abstract notion ("a hollow/receptacle that holds and presents its content outward") and then re-read the verbs through that abstraction — but that shift is post-hoc, leans on external lexicography (شكوة = waterskin) and on the contested loanword status of mishkāt, both of which are inadmissible as packet-internal evidence. The grievance residue is therefore falsifiably absent here.

$nA.candidate_root_contribution: Active detestation/aversion directed at a human target — an affectively charged hatred that spurns and rejects its object (person or group), tilting toward hostile impulse rather than neutral dislike.
$nA.plain_explanation: All three occurrences of ش ن ا name hatred/detestation aimed at people. In 108:3 the active participle شانئك is "the one who detests you" — a personal enemy defined by his hatred. In 5:2 and 5:8 the verbal noun شنآن قوم is "detestation of a people," a feeling the believers are warned not to let drive them into transgression or injustice. Whether realized as the agent (the hater) or the abstract affect (the hating), the constant contribution is directed, active hatred toward a human target.
$nA.strongest_counterexample: 5:2 شنآن قوم أن صدوكم — here the hatred has a stated cause (their having barred you from the Sacred Mosque), so one might read the word as "grievance/resentment over a wrong" rather than pure hatred. But the syntax makes شنآن the emotion that could "drive you to transgress," i.e., a detestation of the people that must be restrained; the cause-clause modifies why the hatred exists, not what the word means. Residue holds.

qwl.candidate_root_contribution: Issuing (or being the issuer/product of) a determinate, content-individuated utterance: a "saying" whose specific content can be quoted, referenced anaphorically, or evaluated. The root contributes the pairing of a sayer with statable content — not the physical vocalization, not the address-relation, and not the faculty of articulation.
qwl.plain_explanation: Across all 1722 occurrences, qwl always presents someone (God, humans, angels, jinn, an ant, a hoopoe, skins, the heavens and earth, Hell) as producing a statement whose content is either quoted directly (the overwhelming pattern: qala/qul/yaqulu + direct quote), pointed back to (qalaha 39:50; qa'iluha 23:100; wa-qilihi 43:88), or held up for evaluation as a content-object (qawl ma'ruf 2:263; asdaq qila 4:122; aqwam qila 73:6; qawluhum bi-afwahihim 9:30; munkar min al-qawl 58:2). The noun qawl/qil names the statement itself; the participle qa'il names its bearer; the passive qila/yuqal backgrounds the sayer while keeping the stated content; Form V taqawwala (52:33, 69:44) adds "manufacture statements from oneself" (fabrication, with al-aqawil as the fabricated statements), leaving the same content-bearing residue. Crucially, the root does NOT require audible vocalization: Yusuf's qala in 12:77 is explicitly kept secret in himself (asarraha fi nafsihi wa-lam yubdiha), and 58:8 has yaquluna fi anfusihim — the saying is internal yet still has quotable content. Conversely, when the Quran wants the physical or faculty layer it uses other roots right next to qwl: ma yalfizu min QAWLIN (50:18 — lafz = emission, qawl = the statement emitted) and the skins' qalu antaqana Allah (41:21 — nutq = granted articulation, qwl = the act of stating). Divine decree uses (haqqa l-qawlu 36:7; 32:13 where the decree's content is quoted in the same verse: la-amla'anna jahannam) and the creative kun (2:117, 16:40, 36:82) are still determinate statements. Even the idiom-like yuqalu lahu Ibrahim (21:60) is a habitual statement whose content is the name. No occurrence uses qwl for mere sound, noise, or contentless expression.
qwl.strongest_counterexample: 21:60 "yuqalu lahu Ibrahim" (a youth called/named Ibrahim) is the most bleached use — closest to a naming idiom rather than an act of stating. It reconciles because the passive habitual yuqal still frames a recurrent statement whose quoted content is the name itself ("it is said of him: Ibrahim"). Second-strongest pressure: 19:34 "qawla l-haqq" where on one reading qawl designates Jesus himself; on either canonical construal (the true statement about him, or Jesus as realization of God's statement — cf. the kun pattern 2:117, 16:40) the content-individuated-statement residue remains present, so neither case breaks universal presence.

kwn.candidate_root_contribution: The obtaining of a state of affairs: an entity standing actualized in a determinate condition, identity, or position — 'being-so' as realized fact (or, negated/commanded, as fact denied or brought to obtain) — rather than any agentive action.
kwn.plain_explanation: Across all 1390 occurrences, kwn never names an action someone performs on something; it always asserts that a situation holds (or comes to hold, or fails to hold). The perfect asserts an established state (33:1 'inna Allāha kāna ʿalīman ḥakīman'; 21:30 'kānatā ratqan'); the imperfect asserts a state coming to obtain (101:4 'yawma yakūnu al-nāsu ka-l-farāsh'); the imperative commands a state into obtaining (16:40, 2:117 'kun fa-yakūn'; 2:65 'kūnū qiradatan'); the negation denies that being obtained at all (19:67 'wa-lam yaku shayʾan' — 'he was not a thing', a fully existential use); the deontic 'mā kāna li-X an…' (19:35, 3:79) denies that a state lies within X's proper compass of being. The nouns carry the same residue into the 'where' dimension: makān is the locus in which something's being is instantiated — including substitutive and status uses that outrun bare geometry (12:78 'take one of us in his makān', 28:82 'those who yesterday coveted his makān') — and makānat is one's standing, the position in which one is (39:39/6:135 'act according to your makānat', 36:67 'We would have transformed them ʿalā makānatihim'). Subtract the maf ʿal place-pattern and the abstract-feminine pattern, and the residue 'position-of-being' remains non-empty in every nominal occurrence.
kwn.strongest_counterexample: The nominal cluster makān/makānat (30 N + 2 LOC): 'place' looks semantically remote from copular 'be', and a hostile reading treats makān as an unrelated concrete-place lexeme. It survives because the packet's own uses exceed bare geometry: 12:78 'khudh aḥadanā makānahu' (occupy his position/stead), 28:82 'tamannaw makānahu' (coveted his standing), 39:39 and 6:135 'iʿmalū ʿalā makānatikum' (act from the standing you are in), 36:67 'la-masakhnāhum ʿalā makānatihim' (transformed where/as they stand) — all of which read as 'the position in which one's being is instantiated', exactly the maf'al of the verbal residue. A secondary hard case, divine-attribute kāna (33:1 'kāna ʿalīman ḥakīman'), threatens an inceptive reading of the root ('came to be') but not the preferred residue, since inception was assigned to the imperative/context layer, not the root.

nwr.candidate_root_contribution: Self-manifesting radiance: an active source or emission that makes itself and its surroundings perceptible through glow/light. Lexicalized three ways in the corpus: nār = the radiant (combusting) entity itself; nūr = the emitted/received radiance; munīr (Form IV) = imparting radiance.
nwr.plain_explanation: All 194 occurrences token one of three lexemes — nār "fire" (~145), nūr "light" (~43), munīr "radiance-giving" (6) — and each one names something whose defining property is that it shows itself by glowing. Fire in this corpus is consistently the seen, kindled, blazing entity: Moses perceives it from afar as a beacon (20:10, 27:7, 28:29), it illuminates its surroundings (2:17), molten iron becomes "fire" exactly when it glows (18:96), a sacrifice's acceptance is signaled by fire visibly consuming it (3:183). Light (nūr) is radiance detached from combustion: the moon (10:5, 71:16), God's light (24:35), revelation (5:15, 42:52), the believers' light running before them (57:12, 66:8), always opposed to darkness (2:257, 6:1). The bridge is internal: in 2:17 a kindled nār "illuminates" and its output is immediately called their nūr; in 24:35 nār and nūr co-occur in one radiance economy ("light upon light"). One root, one contribution: radiant self-manifestation; whether it burns (nār) or only shines (nūr) is lexeme- and context-level elaboration.
nwr.strongest_counterexample: 2:174 (with parallel 4:10): "they eat nothing into their bellies but al-nār" — fire located inside bellies, unseen, where visible radiance seems absent and only harm/consumption is in view. Resolution: the root supplies the inherently radiant entity, and the construction is a disclosure claim — what they swallow IS (already, in reality) the Fire that will manifest; concealment-now is the rhetorical point (katama 'concealing' is the very sin named in the verse), and the eschatological manifestation is explicit in the sequel (wa-sayaṣlawna saʿīran, 4:10). The token still denotes the radiant entity, deployed as latent. This is the hardest case; it bends but does not break the residue.

Dll.candidate_root_contribution: Loss of the connecting way/track between an entity and its intended target, such that arrival or retrieval fails. Two symmetrical faces of one relation: subject-side, a mover (person, deed, effort, memory-item, body) no longer holds the line to its goal and so does not arrive (astray, wasted, forgotten); observer-side, the entity drops off the seeker's track and becomes unfindable/unavailable (vanished, of no avail). Form IV adds causation of this track-loss; the nouns name the resulting off-track state.
Dll.plain_explanation: Across all 191 occurrences the root marks one situation: something that should be connected to a destination by a way loses that way. A person strays from God's path (dalla 'an sabilihi, 16:125, 68:7); a fabricated deity 'strays away from' its worshippers, i.e. cannot be found or reached when needed (dalla 'anhum ma kanu yaftarun, 10:30 and nine parallels; 7:37 dallu 'anna); deeds and effort 'stray', i.e. never arrive at their reward (18:104; 47:1 adalla a'malahum, negated in 47:4); a witness 'strays' from a memory item until the other reminds her (2:282); God never 'strays' from what is recorded nor forgets (20:52); dead bodies 'stray in the earth', becoming untraceable (32:10); a plot is put into tadlil, made to travel without arriving (105:2). The constant antonym pairing with h-d-y (guidance along a way) in dozens of verses confirms the residue: not moral evil as such, but way-loss relative to a target — with religion, morality, memory, or physical location supplied by context.
Dll.strongest_counterexample: 20:52 'la yadillu rabbi wa-la yansa' (My Lord does not dall nor forget) — no path, no morality, no misguidance is available here, so any 'religious error' hypothesis fails outright. It survives only under the track-loss residue: knowledge is in a record, and God never loses the track to any item in it; the pairing with nasiya (forget) confirms dall as retrieval-failure. Same pressure from 2:282 ('an tadilla ihdahuma fa-tudhakkir...' — a witness losing the memory-track, cured by reminding) and 32:10 (bodies dall in the earth = untraceable).

smE.candidate_root_contribution: Auditory intake: the reception of an emitted vocal/sonic signal into a perceiver, an intake that inherently positions the receiver for uptake or response (the response itself is always supplied by context, never by the root).
smE.plain_explanation: Across all 185 occurrences the root marks one thing: a signal that is sounded reaches and enters a receiver. Form I is the bare intake event — hearing speech (2:75, 58:1), raw sounds (19:98 rikz, 20:108 hams, 21:102 hasis, 67:7 shahiq, 50:42 sayhah), or a circulating report with bi- (12:31, 23:24, 28:36, 38:7). The noun samE names the intake faculty/channel itself, listed alongside sight and heart as an accountable instrument (2:7, 16:78, 17:36, 32:9, 41:20-22, 46:26) and as the access-channel to celestial speech that jinn try to tap (15:18, 26:212, 72:9). samiyE (divine name ~45x, human 76:2) is the standing attribute of that intake — pointedly paired with what is uttered: qawl (58:1), duEa' (3:38, 14:39), tahawur (58:1). Form VIII (istamaEa, 18x) adds deliberate directedness to the intake (7:204, 20:13, 39:18, 46:29); Form V (37:8) adds strained repeated attempts at illicit intake; the intensive sammaEuwna (5:41-42, 9:47) adds habitual avidity; Form IV (15x) causes intake in another (27:80, 30:52, 35:22, 8:23). The covenant formula samiEna wa-'aTaEna (2:285, 24:51) and its inversion wa-EaSayna (2:93, 4:46) prove the residue is intake and not obedience: hearing is coordinated WITH obeying/disobeying as a separate act, so heeding is contextual, not root-borne. Likewise 8:21 (they said samiEna but la yasmaEuwna) grades depth of intake polemically — the root contribution (signal reception) is present in both tokens; the verse denies that the intake was real, it does not use the root for something other than intake.
smE.strongest_counterexample: 25:12 — samiEuw laha taghayyuZan wa-zafiyran: "they hear from it fury and roaring." Fury (taghayyuZ) is not itself a sound, so this token could be read as smE covering non-auditory perception, which would break the residue. Resolution stays internal: taghayyuZ is coordinated with zafiyr (an explicit sound) under one verb, and the parallel Fire-passages in the same packet give the Fire an audible voice (67:7 shahiyq "they heard its inhaling roar", 21:102 Hasiys, 50:42). The fury is received through its sonic manifestation — a coordination/zeugma effect at the construction layer, not a shift in root contribution. Second-hardest: 8:21, resolved above as contextual grading of intake depth.

Hyy.candidate_root_contribution: Animate vitality: the state or force of being a living, self-moving, responsive-sentient existent, in categorical opposition to mawt/inertness — covering (a) the state itself (ḥayāh), (b) its bearer (ḥayy/ḥayyah), (c) its conferral (Form IV), (d) its verbal invocation upon another (Form II taḥiyyah), and (e) its reflexive enactment (Form X: seeking another's staying-alive, or the living self's own felt sensitivity/recoil).
Hyy.plain_explanation: Across all 184 confirmed occurrences the root contributes one thing: aliveness as active, responsive vitality opposed to deadness. In ~70 al-ḥayāt al-dunyā verses it names the current state of vital existence (always shadowed by the ākhirah contrast); in the ḥayy cluster it names bearers of that state, including God as al-Ḥayy (2:255) whose vitality excludes even sleep; Form IV (51x) is the conferral of that vitality — on the dead (36:79), the earth (30:24), or the already-alive who are quickened further (8:24, 16:97), showing the residue is scalar vitality, not the mere status of not-being-dead. The serpent of 20:20 is named ḥayyah exactly at the moment inert wood becomes a self-moving thing (tasʿā). The greeting cluster (taḥiyyah/ḥayyā) is Form II declarative: pronouncing continued life/flourishing on someone — the Quran itself repeatedly gives its content as salām (10:10, 14:23, 33:44, 25:75). Form X splits by construction: with a personal object it is seeking that someone stay alive (the six Pharaoh verses); with an an-/min- complement it is the living self's own vital sensitivity turned inward as restraint (2:26, 33:53, 28:25).
Hyy.strongest_counterexample: The diffidence cluster — 2:26 (Allah lā yastaḥyī an yaḍriba mathalan), 33:53 (fa-yastaḥyī minkum / lā yastaḥyī mina l-ḥaqq), 28:25 (tamshī ʿalā istiḥyāʾ) — where no death-contrast appears and 'life' is least visible on the surface. It is reconciled internally by the Form X construction split (the same morphological shape carries 'keep alive' in 2:49, 7:127, 7:141, 14:6, 28:4, 40:25 with personal objects) and by 33:53's own contrast structure, reading the restraint as the sentient living self's responsiveness; but this reconciliation is form-mediated inference, not direct contextual demonstration, and it caps the result at MODERATE.

swE.candidate_root_contribution: A delimited unit-slice of time: a bounded portion of time grasped as a single indivisible occasion that arrives and passes as a whole — a discrete temporal "now" whose onset can be scheduled, awaited, missed, or come suddenly, and whose extent is fixed by context rather than by the root.
swE.plain_explanation: Everywhere this root appears as a common noun it names a chunk of time treated as one sealed unit. Indefinite, it is the minimal such chunk: sinners feel they stayed only "a sāʿah of a day" (10:45, 46:35, 30:55), and no nation can slip "a sāʿah" behind or ahead of its fixed term (7:34, 10:49, 16:61, 34:30). In construct, it can be a specific historical episode, "the sāʿah of hardship" (9:117). With the definite article in eschatological discourse it becomes THE unit of time par excellence — the appointed Hour that draws near (54:1), stands up (30:12, 30:14, 30:55, 40:46, 45:27), and arrives suddenly (6:31, 12:107, 22:55, 43:66, 47:18, 7:187), with knowledge of its timing reserved to God (7:187, 31:34, 33:63, 41:47, 43:85, 79:42). In all these the discourse is about the time-point's arrival and scheduling — exactly what a bounded-time-unit root predicts. The one occurrence where this cannot be internally demonstrated is the idol name Suwāʿ (71:23), a proper noun.
swE.strongest_counterexample: 71:23 (Suwāʿ, idol proper name): no internal evidence connects an idol's name to the temporal residue; it is unassessable, not merely difficult. Among common nouns, the strongest stress is 9:117 "sāʿat al-ʿusrah," where the referent is an extended campaign episode, not a short moment — this falsifies any "instant/60-minutes" reading and forces the residue to be "bounded slice treated as one occasion" (duration contextual); under that phrasing 9:117 is fully consistent.

Avm.candidate_root_contribution: Culpable guilt-charge: a blameworthy liability that accrues to and is borne by an accountable agent, registering against him as an earned debit that makes him answerable to requital.
Avm.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences the root does not name harm done to others or mere error; it names the guilt-debit that an act (or inner state) charges to its doer's own account. The packet's own grammar shows this: ithm is earned (kasaba/iktasaba 4:111, 4:112, 24:11, 6:120), carried (iḥtamala 4:112, 33:58), borne away with (tabūʾa bi-ithmī wa-ithmika 5:29), deserved/incurred (istaḥaqqā ithman 5:107), increased as a balance (li-yazdādū ithman 3:178), and rests "upon" someone or not (fa-lā ithma ʿalayhi 2:173, 2:182, 2:203; ithmuhu ʿalā alladhīna yubaddilūnahu 2:181). It attaches even to purely inner acts (baʿḍu al-ẓanni ithm 49:12; āthimun qalbuhu 2:283; ẓāhir al-ithm wa-bāṭinahu 6:120), confirming that the residue is culpability charged to the person rather than external damage. Objects can contain guilt-generating potential (wine/gambling: fīhimā ithmun kabīr 2:219), whose exact negation is the paradise drink that produces lā taʾthīm (52:23, 56:25). The agent forms name the bearer (āthim 2:283, 5:106, 76:24) and the habitual accumulator (athīm 7x), and athām (25:68) names the moment the accumulated liability falls due.
Avm.strongest_counterexample: 25:68 "wa-man yafʿal dhālika yalqa athāman" — here the word denotes the penal consequence met, not the wrongful charge itself, so the residue is not an act-description at all. It reconciles only after a pattern-layer subtraction: faʿāl as outcome-noun, the guilt-debit falling due ("meets" fits a consequence, not an act). Secondary candidate: 2:219 predicates ithm of objects (wine and gambling contain "great ithm"), where no agent is on stage; resolved as the guilt-liability the things generate for their users, supported internally by the paradise-wine mirror "lā taʾthīm" (52:23, 56:25).

TEm.candidate_root_contribution: Oral intake of sustenance into the body: the taking-in of nourishment (solid or liquid), the substance so taken in, or the quality sensed upon taking it in.
TEm.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences the root marks the intake side of nourishment. As the noun ṭaʿām it names whatever is taken in as sustenance — ordinary provisions (12:37, 18:19, 2:61), lawful/unlawful classes of it (3:93, 5:5, 5:96, 6:145), what messengers eat proving embodiment (21:8, 25:7, 25:20, 5:75), expiation portions (2:184, 5:95), and even hell's anti-foods, which are still ingested (44:44, 69:36, 73:13, 88:6). As the Form I verb it is direct intake — crucially including water at 2:249 ('man lam yaṭʿamhu' of the river), so the invariant is intake, not solid food. Form IV adds only causation (feed = cause another's intake: 106:4, 76:8-9, 74:44, 6:14), Form X adds only request (18:77 'they asked its people for food'), and ṭaʿm at 47:15 is the quality perceived on intake (the milk's taste). Subtracting those form-layers, every occurrence keeps the same residue: nourishment entering the body by mouth.
TEm.strongest_counterexample: 2:249 ('wa-man lam yaṭʿamhu fa-innahu minnī'), where the object is river water — a genuine counterexample to any 'solid food' hypothesis, and the strongest pressure on this one. It is reconciled because the verse itself opposes shariba (drink freely) to lam yaṭʿamhu (take none of it in at all, even a taste): the root's intake sense, not a food-substance sense, is exactly what the contrast requires. 47:15 (ṭaʿm of milk, a liquid) independently confirms the liquid-inclusive intake/taste reading.

qdm.candidate_root_contribution: Fore-position on an ordered axis: being, coming, or placing at the front/ahead, prior to what follows — covering spatial leading-position and temporal anteriority as one axis, systematically opposed to '-x-r (behind/later).
qdm.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences the root marks "the ahead-slot." Form II qaddama (27x) = cause something to occupy the slot ahead of you: deeds sent forward to meet you at reckoning (bimA qad~amat >aydiyhim, mA qad~amat li-gad 59:18), a charity presented in advance (58:12-13), nothing put forward ahead of God and His Messenger (49:1), a warning sent ahead (50:28). Form V (48:2, 74:37) = move oneself into the ahead-slot vs. lag. Form X (10:49, 16:61, 34:30, 7:34, participle 15:24) = seek to be ahead of an appointed point vs. seek delay. Form I: Pharaoh at the front leading his people (11:98); God advancing upon their deeds (25:23). The noun qadam/aqdAm names the fore-stepping limb — one's advanced stance — hence "make firm our feet" in confrontation (2:250, 3:147, 47:7, 8:11), a foot slipping after firmness (16:94), and qadam Sidq, a footing of truth deposited ahead with their Lord (10:2). aqdamUn (26:76) = the more-prior forefathers; qadIm (12:95, 36:39, 46:11) = long-prior, standing since before.
qdm.strongest_counterexample: 41:29 ("najAalhumA taHta aqdAminA" — beneath our feet) and 55:41 (seized by forelocks and feet): here feet are mere body parts, even the lowest point, so the fore-position residue is carried only by the lexicalized noun (the forward-stepping limb) rather than demonstrated by context. Secondary strain: 25:23 "qadimnA ilA mA amilU," where Form I reads as arrival/advancing-upon; presence requires reading it as coming into the position before/at their deeds.

x$y.candidate_root_contribution: Apprehension proportioned to the appraised weight of its object: an estimation-grounded, object-directed fear of a source or eventuality judged to have power over one's outcomes, which operates without the threat being perceptually present (بالغيب, أن-clauses about projected futures) and which regulates present conduct (withholding, yielding, compliance, preemptive action).
x$y.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences, خشي is never fear of a present, perceived danger; it is always apprehension keyed to an APPRAISAL of what its object could do or bring about. Three corpus-internal signals establish this. (1) Knowledge-linkage: 35:28 makes خشية of God the mark of العلماء specifically; 79:19 sequences guidance-to-the-Lord then فتخشى; the reminder cluster (20:3, 20:44, 79:26, 87:10) treats خشية as the receptivity that a تذكرة/عبرة activates. Fear here follows from knowing/estimating the object's weight. (2) Absence-compatibility: خشية repeatedly takes unseen or future objects — the Lord بالغيب (21:49, 35:18, 36:11, 50:33, 67:12), a Day (31:33), the Hour (79:45), and projected eventualities via أن-clauses (18:80, 20:94, 5:52) or anticipated states (إملاق 17:31, الإنفاق 17:100, كساد 9:24, العنت 4:25). (3) Conduct-regulation: خشية explains withholding spending (17:100), infanticide (17:31), hypocrites' alliances (5:52), preemptive intervention (18:80), Aaron's inaction (20:94), and is what the allocation-correction imperatives redirect (فلا تخشوهم واخشون 2:150, 5:3, 5:44; الله أحق أن تخشاه 33:37, 9:13; لم يخش إلا الله 9:18; لا يخشون أحدا إلا الله 33:39). Because it is appraisal-based, it is gradable and comparable (4:77 كخشية الله أو أشد خشية) and can be misallocated — the corpus's recurrent polemic is precisely about re-ranking whose weight one apprehends. The inanimate cases (stones falling من خشية الله 2:74; the mountain crumbling 59:21) confirm the residue is response-to-appraised-overwhelming-weight rather than a merely human emotion.
x$y.strongest_counterexample: 18:80 (فخشينا أن يرهقهما طغيانا وكفرا): the speaker is the "We" of the Khidr narrative, and attributing a raw fear-emotion there strains. It is reconciled only under the appraisal-based formulation — an estimation of a weighty projected outcome motivating preemptive action — whose أن-clause construction exactly parallels the uncontroversial human cases 20:94 (خشيت أن تقول) and 5:52 (نخشى أن تصيبنا). Secondary pressure comes from 2:74 and 59:21 (stones/mountain من خشية الله), where "anticipation of future harm" strains but "yielding response to appraised overwhelming weight" holds; these two cases actively support the weight-appraisal residue over a narrow emotion reading.

Ejl.candidate_root_contribution: Forward displacement in time relative to a due term: bringing about, seeking, or embodying the arrival of something BEFORE its appointed/completed measure (the counter-pole of >jl 'appointed term' and t-A-x-r 'deferral').
Ejl.plain_explanation: Across all 47 occurrences the root marks not mere speed but prematurity — something pulled ahead of a set point of completion. Form X (19x + its verbal noun) is always "demanding God's threatened decree arrive before its term," and the verses themselves supply the term being violated (ajal musamman 29:53, ajaluhum 10:11, maw'id 18:58, qabla yawmi al-hisab 38:16, min qabli an yuqda ilayka wahyuhu 20:114). Form II is delivering a thing early (advance payment of this-life share 17:18, early portion of promised spoils 48:20). The base verb is acting ahead of a running count or an incomplete process (19:84, 20:84, 75:16). al-'ajilah is "the life that arrives first" opposed to the deferred heavy day (76:27). 'ajal (21:37) names the disposition itself, with explicit root wordplay. The calf ('ijl, 10x) reads as the pre-mature bovine, and the Quran itself welds the idol-calf to root-haste verbs: a'jalaka/'ajiltu (20:83-84) directly precede the calf of 20:88, and 7:150 indicts the calf-takers with a-'ajiltum amra rabbikum — the calf is the artifact of not waiting out the forty appointed nights (2:51).
Ejl.strongest_counterexample: 'ijl "calf" (esp. 11:69, 51:26 where it is simply food offered to guests): the lexeme could be a semantically opaque animal name (a homonym or borrowing) with no live temporal content. It is reconciled as "the not-yet-mature bovine" plus the packet-internal coupling of the calf narrative to root-haste verbs (20:83-88, 7:150, 2:51's forty nights; even 11:69 is framed by fa-ma labitha and 51:26 by faragha), but the temporal residue in the bare noun is plausible rather than independently demonstrable from verse text alone.

bdA.candidate_root_contribution: First-onset: performing the initial instance of an act or process, occupying the first position in an ordered (and typically iterable) sequence — an onset defined relative to what follows it (a next stage, a repetition, or a return).
bdA.plain_explanation: Across all 15 occurrences, b-d-ʾ marks "doing X for the first time / as the first step." Ten tokens sit in the creation formula "He begins the creation, then repeats it" (10:4, 10:34 twice, 21:104, 27:64, 29:19, 29:20, 30:11, 30:27, 32:7), where the root supplies the first pass of a process whose second pass is named by ʿ-w-d or by "the latter production" (29:20). The two human-agent uses make the ordinal sense explicit: Joseph "began with their bags BEFORE his brother's bag" (12:76) — first item in a series — and the enemies "initiated against you THE FIRST TIME" (9:13). The absolute uses (85:13 "He originates and repeats", 7:29 "as He first made you, you will return") and the negation (34:49 "falsehood neither originates nor repeats") trade on the same first-versus-again polarity. The root never describes the manner of making — only that this is the first performance.
bdA.strongest_counterexample: 12:76 (فَبَدَأَ بِأَوْعِيَتِهِمْ قَبْلَ وِعَاءِ أَخِيهِ): the only occurrence with no repetition or return anywhere in view — the search is a one-time event. It falsifies any residue phrased as "onset destined for repetition." It is reconciled only under the weaker, ordinal formulation ("first position in an ordered sequence," here marked by qabla), which is why the residue was framed that way.

unreconciled_occurrences: 22:40 (word_ref 22:40:20:2, biyaʿ = worship-houses: root contribution recoverable only as naming-motivation via the internally attested God-ward exchange of 9:111/48:10, not demonstrably present as live synchronic meaning)
byE.candidate_root_contribution: A ratified reciprocal hand-over: two parties each relinquish something of value to the other under agreed terms, sealing a binding, finalized exchange-compact (whether the counter-values are goods/price or selves-and-allegiance/reward-and-protection).
byE.plain_explanation: Across all 15 occurrences the root marks a two-sided, terms-bearing, sealed exchange. As a bare noun (bayʿ) it names the finalized exchange-event itself: the commercial transaction that ceases on the Last Day (2:254, 14:31), that is licit as against ribā (2:275 twice), that must not distract from or displace remembrance and prayer (24:37, 62:9), and — decisively for the unity claim — the exchange with God in which believers hand over selves and wealth against the Garden (9:111 bi-bayʿikum, explicitly glossed by the verse itself with ishtarā, 'purchased'). Form III (bāyaʿa, 6x: 48:10 twice, 48:18, 60:12 twice, 9:111) is the same exchange directed at a personal counterpart: the pledge scenes, where the hand-imagery is explicit ('the hand of God is above their hands', 48:10) and the terms are itemized ('pledge you ON the condition that they not associate...', 60:12) — allegiance and obedience handed over against acceptance, forgiveness, and reward. Form VI (tabāyaʿtum, 2:282) is the mutual enactment among ordinary parties, embedded in a passage about debts, terms, and witnessing — again exchange-with-ratification (witnesses seal it). The one resistant item is 22:40 (biyaʿ, plural), which denotes a class of worship-buildings; there the root contribution survives only as naming motivation: houses in which the God-ward exchange-compact (the sense fixed internally by 9:111 and 48:10) is enacted and God's name remembered — coherent, but not demonstrably a live synchronic semantics of the word.
byE.strongest_counterexample: 22:40 — biyaʿ appears in a list of demolishable buildings (ṣawāmiʿ, biyaʿ, ṣalawāt, masājid) 'in which God's name is much remembered'. The word denotes a building-type, not an exchange-event; no transaction, parties, or terms are on the surface of the verse. The reconciliation (venues of the covenant-exchange with God) is internally motivated but inferential.

kff.candidate_root_contribution: Checking at a closed boundary: an edge or surface that arrests crossing, so that what is on one side is held from passing to the other — verbally as stopping an advancing force at the line (with ʿan marking the shielded party), nominally as the palm, the body's own stopping-and-holding surface, and in kāffah as a collective whose boundary is sealed shut (no member outside it, none detaching from it).
kff.plain_explanation: The root k-f-f is about a stopping edge. Eight verbal occurrences all describe halting something at a boundary so it cannot reach the other side: God restrains people's hands from the believers (48:20, 48:24, 5:11), restrains the Children of Israel from Jesus (5:110), may restrain the might of the disbelievers (4:84); believers are told to hold back their hands (4:77), hypocrites must withhold theirs (4:91); the disbelievers will be unable to hold the Fire back from their faces (21:39). The two noun occurrences name the palm (kaffayhi, 13:14 and 18:42) — the hand's flat checking-and-holding surface — both in scenes where it fails to retain anything (water that never reaches the mouth, wealth already lost). The five kāffah occurrences (2:208, 34:28, 9:122, 9:36 twice) describe a totality as a closed enclosure: enter peace with all of yourselves inside (2:208), fight and be fought as one unbroken body (9:36), do not march out as an undivided whole (9:122, where kāffah is explicitly opposed to a detached faction), and a mission whose reach closes around all people (34:28). One idea — a boundary that lets nothing cross — runs through restraining, the palm, and totality.
kff.strongest_counterexample: The kāffah cluster, sharpest at 2:208 'udkhulū fī s-silmi kāffatan' — 'enter into peace kāffah' reads on the surface as plain 'entirely/all together,' with no visible act of restraint, and could be claimed as a lexicalized adverb detached from the root. Resolution from inside the corpus: 9:122 opposes kāffah to a firqah/ṭāʾifah that separates out, and 2:208 immediately opposes it to following Satan's khuṭuwāt (step-by-step leakage out of the whole) — kāffah is totality construed as a sealed boundary, every member held within, which is the same checking-edge residue. The reconciliation works but requires this construal step, which is what caps the result at MODERATE.

mTr.candidate_root_contribution: A shower-descent from the sky onto a target below: a quantity of discrete matter (prototypically water, but substance-unspecified) falling from above in pelting, distributed fashion upon a location or people. The root encodes the manner and directionality of arrival (sky-to-ground, onto), not the substance and not any good/bad valence.
mTr.plain_explanation: In every Quranic occurrence, m-T-r is about something coming down out of the sky onto someone or something beneath it. As a plain noun it names the shower itself — ordinary rain that soldiers may shelter from (4:102), the rain a cloud is hoped to bring (46:24), or the terrible 'rain' that fell on Lot's people (25:40, 26:173, 27:58, 7:84). As a Form IV verb it means causing that shower to fall on a target, always with 'upon' (ʿalā): God rains stones on the condemned towns (11:82, 15:74), or mockers dare God to rain stones on them (8:32). That stones — not water — can be what is 'rained' proves the root is about the mode of falling from the sky onto a target, not about water itself; and the hopeful use in 46:24 and the neutral use in 4:102 prove the root is not inherently about punishment.
mTr.strongest_counterexample: The stone-object uses (11:82:7:2, 15:74:4:2, 8:32:11:2 — amṭarnā/fa-amṭir ʿalayhā/ʿalaynā ḥijāratan) are the hardest for any 'rain = water from the sky' reading, since what falls is stones. They are resolved, not forced: the substance is expressed in a separate object slot, so the root's own contribution must be the shower-manner of sky-to-target descent, which is demonstrably present (stones arrive exactly as a rain does — from above, in quantity, onto a target). No occurrence resists the substance-neutral shower-descent residue.

rkb.candidate_root_contribution: Superposition onto a bearer: one entity comes to be positioned on top of (or fitted onto) a distinct supporting entity that then bears/carries it. Riding is the prototypical case (rider upon animal/ship), but the residue is the mounted-upon-a-support relation itself, not motion or travel.
rkb.plain_explanation: Everywhere rkb appears, something is set upon something else that holds it up: people upon ships (11:41, 11:42, 18:71, 29:65), people upon animals (16:8, 40:79, 36:42, 43:12 — which pairs ships and cattle under one verb, showing the Quran itself treats them as one act), the nominals for mounted people and mounts (2:239 rukbaan vs. rijaal on foot, 36:72 rakuub, 59:6 rikaab, 8:42 al-rakb). The three non-riding cases carry the same relation without travel: grain mutarakib (6:99) is grains stacked one upon another; rakkabaka (82:8) is God fitting/mounting your parts together into a form; 84:19 la-tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq is mounting stage upon stage, where the object tabaq (layer) itself encodes superposition. Subtract the vehicle, the journey, and the grammatical form, and the same residue remains in all fifteen.
rkb.strongest_counterexample: 84:19 (la-tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq): no physical bearer is named and the sense is transitional/eschatological, so a purely physical 'riding' reading cannot be verified from the verse alone. It is reconciled because the object tabaq (layer/stage) itself supplies the stacked-support structure the root requires — mounting onto stage after stage — but it remains the occurrence most dependent on construal.

swm.candidate_root_contribution: Setting forth into the open so as to be visibly borne: an entity is turned out into an exposed domain, or made to carry an openly displayed condition/sign that stays attached to it. The nominal siymaA is the openly borne identifying display; Form II participles denote being endowed with such a display; the Form I verb (double accusative) denotes keeping someone turned out under an imposed condition as their standing lot; Form IV denotes turning animals out into open range.
swm.plain_explanation: Across all 15 occurrences, s-w-m contributes the idea of something being put out in the open and borne there. (a) In all six siymaA tokens (2:273, 7:46, 7:48, 47:30, 48:29, 55:41) it is a visible display carried on a person by which they are recognized — five of the six collocate with the verb '-r-f "recognize" (2:273 taErifuhum bisiymaAhum; 7:46 yaErifuwna kullaan bisiymaAhum; 7:48 yaErifuwnahum bisiymaAhum; 47:30 falaEaraftahum bisiymaAhum; 55:41 yuErafu Almujrimuwna bisiymaAhum), and 48:29 locates it explicitly on the exposed surface, "siymaAhum fiy wujuwhihim min 'avari Alssujuwdi", after taraAhum "you see them". (b) The four Form II derivatives (11:83, 51:34 stones musaw~amap Einda rab~ika; 3:125 angels musaw~imiyna; 3:14 horses Almusaw~amap) denote entities made to bear such a display — the stones' marking designates them for their targets (lilmusrifiyna, 51:34). (c) The four Form I verbs (2:49, 7:141, 14:6, 7:167) all use the identical double-accusative frame yasuwmuwna-hum/yasuwmu-hum suw'a AlEa*aAbi: the victims are held turned-out under evil punishment as their imposed, continuing condition (imperfect aspect throughout; 7:167 extends it 'ilaY yawmi AlqiyaAmap). (d) The single Form IV (16:10 fiyhi tusiymuwna) is the causative of the same setting-forth: you turn livestock out into the open growth. The root residue is thus not "punish", "graze", or "sign" as such, but the open setting-forth/borne-exposure that each of those readings instantiates.
swm.strongest_counterexample: 16:10 (tusiymuwna): the pastoral token has no in-text marking or recognition dimension at all; it only fits if the residue is pitched at "turning out into the open" rather than "identifying mark". It is the occurrence that forces the abstraction level up and is therefore the best lever for falsifying the unified residue.

$yb.candidate_root_contribution: Whitening/greying of the head's hair as the visible bodily marker of depleted vitality — the chromatic sign of the late, post-strength stage of life (not old age itself, but its appearance on the head).
$yb.plain_explanation: Across all three occurrences the root supplies one thing: white/grey head-hair as the outward sign that vital strength has passed. In 19:4 Zakariyya's head has "ignited" with it alongside weakened bones; in 30:54 it names the stage after strength, conjoined with weakness; in 73:17 the terror of the Day imposes this very sign on children — they are made white-haired, not made old, which proves the root contributes the visible marker rather than chronological age.
$yb.strongest_counterexample: 73:17 is the only candidate stressor: one could claim shīb there means merely "aged ones," making the root "old age" rather than "white hair." But the verse's force is precisely the visual inversion — children bearing the white-hair sign without lived age — so the occurrence resists the "old age" reading and instead confirms the chromatic-marker residue. No occurrence is inconsistent with the proposed contribution.

*Ab.candidate_root_contribution: The wild predatory canid — the wolf as a concrete entity; in its Quranic deployment, the solitary predator whose threat attaches specifically to a human charge left without guard.
*Ab.plain_explanation: All three occurrences are the single definite noun al-dhi'b ("the wolf") inside the Yusuf narrative (12:13, 12:14, 12:17). In every occurrence the wolf is the subject of "devour" (akala) with Yusuf as object, and in every occurrence the devouring is non-actual: feared by Yaqub (12:13), hypothesized by the brothers (12:14), and falsely alleged by them (12:17). The wolf never appears on-scene; it exists only within speech about an unwitnessed event. The stable root contribution across all three is the concrete wolf-entity as the paradigmatic danger to the unguarded.
*Ab.strongest_counterexample: None exists in the confirmed set. The nearest candidate for tension is 12:17, where the wolf's act is a fabrication — but the fabricated status belongs to the speech-act context, not the root: the lie only works because the wolf-entity is a plausible devourer, which presupposes rather than contradicts the proposed contribution.

*qn.candidate_root_contribution: The chin: the frontal underside terminus of the face at its junction with the neck — the body's pivot-point that marks the extreme limit of head inclination, downward (face driven fully to the ground) or upward (head forced back so it cannot bow).
*qn.plain_explanation: All three occurrences are the same plural noun al-adhqan in a prepositional frame, and in each the chins function as a limit-line of head posture. In 17:107 and 17:109 those given knowledge "fall to the chins" (yakhirruna li-l-adhqan) — prostration pressed past the forehead to the lowest frontal point of the face, intensified by sujjadan/yabkuna/khushu'an. In 36:8 iron collars on the necks reach "up to the chins" (ila l-adhqan), so the wearers are muqmahun — heads forced up, unable to lower the face. The same referent thus anchors both extremes: chins to the ground in voluntary humility, chins propped up in enforced inability to humble. The root's contribution (the chin as the terminal frontal point of the face/head) is present and doing work in every occurrence; the polarity (down vs. up) comes from construction (li- of falling vs. ila of upper bound) and context, not from the root.
*qn.strongest_counterexample: 36:8 is the only candidate for resistance: chins there are pushed UP, the apparent opposite of the falling-down usage in 17:107/109. But the root supplies the same referent in both; the opposed directions come from ila (collar's upper limit) vs. kharra li- (collapse onto), so 36:8 confirms rather than breaks the residue — the chin is precisely the line the collar must reach to prevent the bowing that 17:107/109 describe. No occurrence resists the proposed contribution.

*rw.candidate_root_contribution: A sweeping, wind-like agency that lifts light or loose matter and carries it away into scattered, irrecoverable dispersion (winnowing-away): the event necessarily involves (a) a moving carrier-agent, (b) a light/particulate patient, and (c) an endpoint of dissipation rather than placement.
*rw.plain_explanation: All three occurrences describe the same event seen through different grammatical lenses. In 18:45 the winds (explicit agent الرياح) sweep away dried plant debris (هشيم) — the verb تذروه with its object suffix shows a transitive act of carrying-off-into-dispersion, sealing the parable of worldly life ending in dissipation. In 51:1 the same event is packaged twice: الذاريات is the agent-participle ('the ones who scatter-carry', internally identifiable as winds via the 18:45 parallel, the only other root occurrence), and ذروا is the cognate masdar intensifying that very event. Subtract the oath construction and the parable context and the identical residue remains in every token.
*rw.strongest_counterexample: None found in the full set. The nearest candidate for resistance is 51:1 الذاريات, whose referent is not named in the verse; but the root contribution itself is secured internally by the exact agent-verb parallel in 18:45 (الرياح ... تذروه), and the cognate accusative ذروا confirms the event-type independent of referent identification. It does not break universal presence.

ASr.candidate_root_contribution: A binding constraint imposed on a bearer from outside: an obligation experienced as a tying load that rests upon the one bound, laid on, contracted, or lifted off by another party.
ASr.plain_explanation: In all three Quranic occurrences, iṣr names something that sits *upon* a party and both weighs on them and binds them. In 2:286 it is a load a Lord may lay upon a community (ḥamala ʿalā), as on earlier communities; in 3:81 it is the binding grip of God's covenant that the prophets take upon themselves by affirming; in 7:157 it is what the Messenger lifts off his followers, paired with shackles (aghlāl). The root's contribution is the fusion of burden and bond: an imposed obligation felt as a constraining weight — never a self-acquired load (that is wizr) and never the pact-event itself (that is mīthāq).
ASr.strongest_counterexample: 3:81 (word_ref 3:81:25:1) is the most resistant: a plain 'heavy burden' reading is strained there, since iṣrī denotes the covenant commitment the prophets affirm. It is reconciled without forcing because the covenant is explicitly taken ʿalā ('upon') them — the residue 'imposed binding constraint resting on a bearer' is demonstrably present; only the pure-weight competitor fails, not the proposed residue.

Abl.candidate_root_contribution: Massed aggregation: a plurality of living units apprehended and handled as one collective body (herd/swarm/wave-mass), such that the many are construed grammatically and referentially as a single unit.
Abl.plain_explanation: The root surfaces in two lexemes: al-'ibil "the camel-kind" (6:144, 88:17) and abaabiil "in massed groups" (105:3). What survives subtraction of form and context in all three is not "camel" (birds in 105:3 refute that) but aggregation-as-unity. In 105:3 birds are sent as massed groups acting en bloc; in 88:17 the plural referent takes a feminine SINGULAR verb (khuliqat — "how IT was created"), showing the multitude construed as one body; in 6:144 the collective class is treated as a single countable kind ("of the 'ibil, two") in parallel with other livestock classes. Every occurrence presents many members packaged as one collective.
Abl.strongest_counterexample: 6:144 is the weakest link for the aggregation hypothesis: the verse itself foregrounds the camel-kind only as a legal category alongside al-baqar, and the aggregation feature is present only via the collective-noun grammar, with no contextual foregrounding of herd-ness. Against the rival "camel-kind" hypothesis, 105:3 (tayran abaabiil — birds, not camels) is a decisive counterexample.
